x.A: Reports stay in S3 Standard for the first week of frequent access, then move to Glacier (Flexible Retrieval), which retrieves within hours and is the cheapest class that meets the 6 hour requirement. Several years of storage costs the least here.
x.B: Standard-IA costs more than Glacier for data that must be kept for years and rarely accessed after the first week.
x.C: Intelligent-Tiering adds a per-object monitoring fee, which is costly for many small 50 KB objects, and its archive tiers must be configured separately.
x.D: Deep Archive retrieval takes up to 12 hours (standard) or 48 hours (bulk), which exceeds the 6 hour limit.

x.A: Reserved Instances for 3 years lock in the instance type and family, but the company changes them every 2 to 3 months.
x.B: A Compute Savings Plan applies across any instance family, size, and Region, so it stays valid when the company changes instance types. A 1 year plan with no upfront payment is flexible.
x.C: All Upfront Reserved Instances are tied to a specific instance type and don't allow changing the family.
x.D: An EC2 Instance Savings Plan is tied to a specific instance family in a Region, so changing the family loses the discount.

x.A: Macie discovers PII in S3. It's a Regional service, so it's enabled in each Region and a discovery job analyzes the buckets there, with no custom code.
x.B: Security Hub aggregates findings, and a Config rule can't analyze the contents of S3 objects for PII.
x.C: Inspector scans for software vulnerabilities and doesn't analyze S3 data for PII.
x.D: GuardDuty detects threats and anomalous activity and doesn't classify the contents of S3 objects as PII.

x.A: Compute optimized instances don't suit an SAP application that has high memory utilization.
x.B: Storage optimized instances are for high I/O workloads, not memory-bound SAP workloads.
x.C: Memory optimized instances (such as R and X families, many certified for SAP) suit both the SAP application and the database, which both have high memory utilization.
x.D: HPC optimized instances are for compute-heavy workloads and don't fit a memory-bound SAP application.

x.A: An interface VPC endpoint (PrivateLink) for SQS in the private subnets gives the instances a private connection to SQS. A security group that allows inbound traffic from the instances controls who can use it.
x.B: Placing the endpoint in the public subnets isn't needed, and the endpoint policy controls actions, not network access from the instances.
x.C: This also uses public subnets, and an SQS access policy referencing a VPC endpoint doesn't set up the network access from the instances.
x.D: SQS doesn't have a gateway endpoint, because gateway endpoints exist only for S3 and DynamoDB, and a NAT gateway sends traffic over the internet.

x.A: A role that can only read can't store user data, and the application needs both read and write access.
x.B: An IAM role with read and write permissions to the tables, added to an instance profile and associated with the application instances, gives the application temporary credentials, so no keys are exposed in the template.
x.C: Entering access and secret keys as template parameters means long-term credentials passed around and exposed.
x.D: Creating an IAM user and passing its keys through user data exposes long-term credentials in the instance, which is insecure.

x.A: Athena queries S3 but doesn't enrich with Redshift data in this way, and splitting the work across Athena and Glue adds complexity.
x.B: EMR processes large semistructured data in S3 in parallel, and it can read from Redshift to enrich the data in the same cluster using Spark.
x.C: Kinesis Data Streams isn't used to move data from S3 into Redshift for enrichment.
x.D: Lake Formation manages access and governance and doesn't enrich data with Redshift data.

x.A: A transit gateway adds hourly and per-GB charges, which is more than needed to connect only two VPCs.
x.B: A Site-to-Site VPN between two VPCs isn't a standard design, it adds cost and complexity, and VPN tunnels have throughput limits.
x.C: VPC peering between VPCs in the same Region has no hourly charge, and data transfer is cheap, so it's the lowest cost for two VPCs and 500 GB a month.
x.D: Direct Connect is for connecting on-premises networks and costs far more.

x.A: AWS generated tags are applied by AWS, such as createdBy, and wouldn't hold the product line information the teams have tagged.
x.B: The teams applied their own tags, so a user-defined tag is the one to select in the Billing console for cost allocation.
x.C: Resource Groups lets you group and find resources by tag, but cost allocation tags are activated in Billing, not Resource Groups.
x.D: Activating tags in each individual account isn't how it works in an organization, because tags are activated in the management account.
x.E: The tag is activated from the Organizations management account so it applies to cost data for all accounts, and consolidated billing shows the cost by product line.

x.A: AWS Control Tower account drift notifications identify changes to the OU hierarchy, such as moved or deleted OUs, and can notify the operations team through SNS. It's built in, so it needs the least effort.
x.B: Config aggregated rules assess resource configuration compliance, not OU structure changes.
x.C: CloudTrail would record the changes, but you'd have to build detection and notifications.
x.D: CloudFormation drift detection applies to stack resources, not to the structure of an organization.

x.A: DAX is a fully managed, in-memory cache built for DynamoDB. It reduces read latency to microseconds, and the application changes only the client endpoint, so it takes little effort.
x.B: ElastiCache for Redis needs application code for the caching logic and cache invalidation, which means more work.
x.C: Memcached has the same problem, and also needs code to populate and invalidate the cache.
x.D: Streams, Lambda, and ElastiCache is a pipeline that you'd build and maintain, so it has the most overhead.

x.A: For a gateway endpoint, you add an entry in the route tables for the subnets so traffic to DynamoDB goes to the endpoint instead of the internet.
x.B: A gateway VPC endpoint for DynamoDB lets instances reach DynamoDB over the AWS network, without going over the internet.
x.C: An interface endpoint for EC2 is for calls to the EC2 API, not DynamoDB.
x.D: Gateway endpoints don't use elastic network interfaces. Interface endpoints do.
x.E: Gateway endpoints don't have security groups, since they're controlled by route tables and endpoint policies.

x.A: Container Insights collects metrics and logs but isn't a central view of both EKS and on-premises clusters.
x.B: EKS Connector registers external Kubernetes clusters, including on-premises ones, in the EKS console, so all clusters and workloads are visible in one place with little effort.
x.C: Systems Manager doesn't give a Kubernetes cluster and workload view.
x.D: EKS Anywhere runs Kubernetes on premises and doesn't act as a view of other clusters.

x.A: EBS encryption protects data at rest, but database administrators or anyone with access can still read the data once it's mounted and in use.
x.B: Client-side encryption with KMS encrypts the data before it reaches the database, so even database administrators can't read the sensitive data. RDS still supports the transactions.
x.C: S3 with server-side encryption doesn't protect against users who have permission to read the objects, and S3 isn't a transactional database.
x.D: Windows file permissions can be changed by administrators, and FSx isn't a transactional database.

x.A: RDS for MySQL with storage scaling grows storage, but it doesn't scale compute automatically for demand.
x.B: Redshift is a data warehouse, not a transactional MySQL-compatible database.
x.C: DMS migrates the database to Aurora, which is MySQL compatible, and Aurora Auto Scaling adds replicas as demand increases, so it's compatible and scales automatically.
x.D: DynamoDB isn't compatible with MySQL applications, which would need to be rewritten.

x.A: S3 is object storage without a real hierarchical file system and isn't suited to rapid concurrent reads and writes as a file system.
x.B: EFS provides a shared, POSIX-compliant file system with a hierarchical directory structure that multiple instances across AZs can read and write at the same time.
x.C: EBS volumes (even Multi-Attach io2) are limited to a single AZ and don't provide a shared file system for instances in two AZs.
x.D: Separate EBS volumes synchronized between instances is complex and doesn't give concurrent, consistent shared access.

x.A: API Gateway with Lambda receives and processes the HTTP data with no servers, and DynamoDB stores it. All are managed, and independent components can be added over time.
x.B: An ELB with EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group means managing servers, which is more overhead.
x.C: A SQL Server Express database on EC2 means managing the database server, which adds overhead.
x.D: EC2 servers and an EFS file system for storing data is more overhead and isn't a good database for the data.

x.A: S3 stores petabytes of data, and CloudFront caches the drawings at edge locations, so users wait less time for them to load.
x.B: Glacier is archive storage with long retrieval times, which isn't suitable for viewing drawings.
x.C: EBS volumes are limited in size and attached to instances, so they can't hold petabytes.
x.D: Storage Gateway is for hybrid environments, and all the application components are in AWS.

x.A: EventBridge publishes metrics to CloudWatch in the AWS/Events namespace, such as MatchedEvents, TriggeredRules, Invocations, and FailedInvocations. They show whether the rule matched and whether the target was invoked.
x.B: A dead-letter queue only has events that failed delivery, and it wouldn't show whether the rule conditions matched.
x.C: EventBridge doesn't write events to CloudWatch Logs by default.
x.D: CloudTrail records API calls, and doesn't show rule matches or target invocations.

x.A: A reminder doesn't scale the instances. Someone would still have to do it manually.
x.B: An Auto Scaling group with a scheduled action raises the capacity to six instances every Friday and reduces it after, automatically with no manual work.
x.C: Manual scaling needs someone to change the capacity each time.
x.D: Automatic (dynamic) scaling reacts to metrics, and doesn't guarantee six instances at the planned time.

x.A: A certificate from the specific third-party CA can be imported into ACM, and an API Gateway custom domain can use it. HTTP APIs support TLS 1.3 on custom domains.
x.B: ACM can't create a certificate that is signed by a third-party CA, since public ACM certificates come from Amazon's CAs.
x.C: ACM can't create a certificate signed by a third-party CA, and a Lambda function URL doesn't let you use a custom certificate.
x.D: ACM can't create third-party certificates, and Lambda function URLs don't support custom certificates.

x.A: DynamoDB isn't MySQL compatible, and the application would need to be rewritten.
x.B: A regular Aurora database has fixed instance capacity and isn't measured in ACUs for auto scaling in this way.
x.C: Aurora Serverless v2 is MySQL compatible and scales capacity automatically in fine-grained ACU steps, with a minimum of 1 ACU (about 2 GiB of memory), so it handles unexpected increases with little administration.
x.D: RDS for MySQL with fixed 2 GiB of memory doesn't scale automatically for unexpected workload increases.

x.A: Provisioned concurrency keeps functions warm and reduces cold starts, but you pay for it all the time, so it costs more.
x.B: A longer timeout doesn't reduce startup latency.
x.C: More memory also adds CPU and may speed up initialization a little, but it doesn't specifically address cold starts and increases cost.
x.D: Lambda SnapStart for Java caches a snapshot of the initialized function, which reduces cold start latency and outliers at no additional cost, so it's the most cost-effective.

x.A: Aurora Serverless v2 scales capacity up and down and can scale to a minimum when idle, so you pay mostly for the 2 hours of use each week.
x.B: A provisioned Aurora cluster runs and bills all week even though it's needed for only 2 hours.
x.C: An EC2 instance with a reservation is billed for the entire time and needs management.
x.D: MySQL containers on ECS keep you managing the database and still cost money while idle.

x.A: DynamoDB isn't PostgreSQL compatible, and global tables solve a different problem.
x.B: Multi-AZ gives high availability but its standby can't serve reads, so there's no increased read capacity.
x.C: A Multi-AZ DB cluster deployment has a writer and two readable standby instances, so it's highly available and adds read capacity through the reader endpoint, in a managed way.
x.D: Cross-Region read replicas add read capacity but don't provide high availability on their own, and add cost and complexity.
